gap: No result ChatGPT got states that none of the cycle counts quoted for solar-light AAs can be compared. Tenergy's 2,000 cycles for both Solla packs and Panasonic's 'up to 2100 times' for eneloop are printed on the maker pages with no test method, depth of discharge or standard, and Tenergy's -4 to 122 °F is a 'working temperature' that does not say whether it covers charging.
standout_why: I compared against the two pages ChatGPT cited. idealgardenlights.com/pages/solar-lights-guide gives no cycle count, self-discharge or temperature figures at all; it only says stock batteries 'can last 1-2 years' and higher-capacity ones '3-5 years'. Tenergy's Solla 1000 page states 'Cycle Life: 2000' and '-4°F to 122°F' with no test condition, and ChatGPT repeated it as is. Neither page explains that the cycle figures come from different or unnamed tests. It scores 2, not 3, because I could not open a Panasonic page with the 2017-test eneloop figure. That figure is the number that would decide the pick, and it is listed under unsourced.
decides: It weakens the 'more rated cycles = longer life' reading of our current table, where eneloop shows 2,100, Solla 2,000, EBL 1,200 and Brightown/Lightalent 1,000. Neither of the two figures I could source names its test, so the column should carry a footnote: 'maker figure, test method not stated'. It should not rank cells by it. If the Panasonic 2017-revision figure (about 600 cycles under IEC 61951-2:2017 7.5.1.4, against 2,100 under the 2011 edition's 7.5.1.3) is confirmed on a Panasonic page, eneloop's cycle advantage over Solla goes away. The pick would then rest on what is sourced: Solla ships pre-charged and makes the only solar-specific overcharge/over-discharge claim, and eneloop states 70% charge retained after 10 years. That confirms Tenergy Solla 1000 as the pick for typical 600–1,000 mAh lights.
